Name: linguistic_budget_titration
Title: Language or Just Length? Titrating the Linguistic Content of Chain-of-Thought to Locate Where Reasoning Truly Needs Words
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning gains from chain-of-thought are driven by two separable ingredients — (a) genuine linguistic/semantic content in the trace and (b) mere additional serial computation length — and by parametrically titrating the linguistic informativeness of the trace while holding token count fixed, we can measure how much of an LLM's 'intelligence' actually requires language versus non-linguistic compute. We hypothesize a task-dependent 'linguistic dependence spectrum': symbolic/arithmetic tasks tolerate heavy delinguification while commonsense/relational tasks collapse, revealing that language is a task-specific scaffold rather than a uniform substrate of reasoning.
Related Work: Wei et al. established CoT; Pfau et al. and Lanham et al. showed filler/dot tokens can partially substitute for reasoning (serial-compute view). COCONUT (Hao et al.) and recent SAE-steering work (He et al. 2026) show latent reasoning can rival explicit CoT, and Zhang et al. 2025 critique latent tokens as shortcut-exploiting pseudo-reasoning. Prior studies treat this as binary — explicit-language vs latent/filler — and mostly on one axis (efficiency or faithfulness). None parametrically TITRATE the linguistic informativeness of the trace along a continuum while holding token count and position fixed, nor map a per-task 'linguistic dependence' spectrum. Our contribution is a controlled dose-response design that decomposes CoT benefits into language-content vs compute-length components, directly quantifying how much reasoning requires language.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves LLM reasoning, but it remains unclear whether the benefit comes from the linguistic content of the reasoning trace or merely from the extra serial computation the extra tokens afford. We introduce a controlled titration methodology that continuously degrades the linguistic informativeness of a reasoning trace while holding token count and position fixed, decomposing CoT's benefit into a language-content component and a compute-length component. We construct a graded sequence of trace types: full natural-language CoT; content-word-only (function words removed); shuffled-content (semantics scrambled but words retained); abstract-symbolic (variables/relations only); and non-linguistic filler tokens of matched length. Across arithmetic, symbolic/algorithmic, multi-hop factual, commonsense, and relational-reasoning benchmarks, we measure accuracy dose-response curves for each trace type using open models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2) via prompting and light supervised finetuning to make models comply with each trace format. We further run causal interventions: (i) selectively corrupting only content-bearing tokens vs function/filler tokens in an otherwise correct trace and measuring answer flips, and (ii) probing hidden states at filler vs content positions to test whether computation happens regardless of linguistic content. We predict a task-dependent linguistic-dependence spectrum: symbolic tasks retain accuracy under heavy delinguification (compute-dominated), while commonsense/relational tasks collapse (language-dominated). Results quantify, per task, how much LLM reasoning genuinely requires language versus non-linguistic serial computation, informing efficient reasoning, faithfulness auditing, and theories of language-thought coupling in AI.
Experiments: 1) TRACE-TYPE CONSTRUCTION: For each of 5 task suites (GSM8K/arithmetic, a synthetic algorithmic/symbolic-manipulation set, HotpotQA multi-hop, CommonsenseQA, and a relational/kinship reasoning set), generate reference CoT traces, then produce 5 graded variants per trace holding token count fixed: (a) full NL CoT, (b) content-words-only, (c) shuffled-content (words retained, order/semantics scrambled), (d) abstract-symbolic (entities->variables, relations->symbols), (e) matched-length filler tokens (e.g., '...'). Verify token-count matching per example. 2) PROMPTING EVALUATION: Instruct 3 open models to reason using each trace format (few-shot demonstrations of the format) and measure final-answer accuracy; build dose-response curves across the language->filler continuum per task. 3) FINETUNING COMPLIANCE: LoRA-finetune each model to reliably emit each trace format (small data, ~2k examples/format) to remove instruction-following confounds, then re-measure. 4) DECOMPOSITION: Fit accuracy = base + beta_len*(#thinking_tokens) + beta_lang*(linguistic_informativeness_score) + task interactions via mixed-effects regression; report per-task beta_lang/beta_len ratio as a 'linguistic dependence index'. 5) CAUSAL TOKEN ABLATION: Given a correct full-NL trace, corrupt (mask/replace) only content-bearing tokens vs only function/filler-position tokens and measure answer-flip rate; predict content corruption flips answers far more on language-dominated tasks. 6) HIDDEN-STATE PROBING: Train linear probes to decode the intermediate answer from hidden states at content vs filler positions; compare decodability to test whether serial compute proceeds independent of linguistic content. METRICS: task accuracy, dose-response slope, linguistic dependence index, answer-flip rate under targeted corruption, probe decoding accuracy. Cross-model and cross-task consistency reported with effect sizes and CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Holding token count fixed while varying informativeness is imperfect (tokenizer differences across formats); mitigated by per-example token matching and reporting token counts as covariates. 2) Models may fail to follow degraded formats via prompting alone; mitigated by LoRA finetuning for compliance. 3) 'Linguistic informativeness score' is an operational proxy; we validate it with human ratings on a sample. 4) Filler-token results may reflect the model covertly still reasoning in latent space rather than true independence from language; the probing experiment directly addresses this but latent-reasoning confounds remain a caveat. 5) Findings may be model-scale-dependent; we test multiple sizes/families and report scaling trends. 6) Synthetic symbolic tasks may not generalize to naturalistic reasoning, so we include multiple naturalistic benchmarks.
